title: Who protects the rules of UK democracy?
label: 11 November 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: The committee examined how the Civil Service Commission, the Ethics and Integrity Commission and the Electoral Commission help protect fair government and elections. Witnesses said the UK has strong foundations, but public trust and those safeguards depend on adequate resources, clear and up-to-date rules, and organisations being able to act independently. They highlighted concerns about political finance, threats and abuse aimed at candidates, complicated election laws, and gaps in oversight of people leaving public service. Members also challenged whether codes and existing standards are enough to prevent serious failures.

chapters.title: How the safeguards work
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses see their organisations as part of the system that supports fair government and trusted elections.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do your organisations form part of the safeguards that protect UK democracy?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: Yes. The Civil Service Commission oversees civil servants throughout their careers: it helps ensure that recruitment is open and based on merit, hears complaints under the Civil Service Code, and advises some civil servants and special advisers on jobs they take after leaving government.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: We also see our role as preventing problems. That means explaining what the rules require and helping the system work properly, not just dealing with complaints after something has gone wrong.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: The Ethics and Integrity Commission looks across the standards system and advises; it doesn't investigate individual cases or regulate people directly. Standards matter because people expect those in public office to use their power fairly and without favouritism.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: We make evidence-based recommendations and help public bodies understand ethical standards. We also learn from Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and from countries facing similar challenges.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: The Electoral Commission provides independent oversight of elections across the UK. Elections give those in power democratic authority and let voters hold them to account, so trusted elections are central to the constitution.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How confident are you that elections are trusted?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: We find high levels of public confidence in how elections are run. Local authorities do most of the practical work, and generally do it efficiently. Political parties also comply with the rules at a high rate, though we can call out breaches and issue fines.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: The weakest area of public confidence is how clearly political money is reported. A bill now before Parliament should make a significant difference. We also need to help people, especially young voters, understand how elections work and how to judge the information they see.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: Abuse and intimidation of candidates is rising. If people are frightened away from standing for election, that weakens democracy. We're testing teaching materials in about 500 schools and hope to reach all schools during 2027.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is that programme just for England?

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: No, it's intended to cover the UK. We're beginning in England and Northern Ireland, where votes at 16 are coming in soon, and will build on work already done in Scotland and Wales.

chapters.title: Pressures on elections
chapters.takeaway: Election officials see growing risks from misleading content, candidate abuse, complex laws and strained local services.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: How well can your organisations protect the system, and what makes that harder?

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: For us, the test is whether good evidence and recommendations are taken up and put into practice. Some earlier recommendations have helped create safeguards, but action can take a long time. I also worry whether we have enough staff and money to do high-quality work as our responsibilities grow.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: The election system faces several serious pressures. One is the flow of misleading or manipulated information, including material produced by foreign actors. During the May 2026 elections, our deepfake detection tool flagged 15 cases that we considered threats to democratic integrity.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: We're not a specialist organisation for detecting manipulated media. We think the state needs a more systematic way to monitor it, so harmful activity can be identified and challenged.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Candidate abuse is another problem. Police responses vary: some forces act, while others struggle to judge where political speech crosses into harassment. That distinction can be difficult, but illegal abuse needs a response.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: People are also uneasy about whether money buys political influence, even though we publish information about where political money comes from. We're reviewing election spending limits and gathering evidence from parties so Parliament can consider what limits make sense.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Election law has accumulated in layers and is now very hard for voters, candidates and election staff to navigate. The new bill may add more complexity. We support work to combine and simplify the rules.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Local authorities remain a strength of the system; we wouldn't replace them. But many are stretched and struggle to provide enough staff and resources for elections. We set standards and identify failures, but councils need the capacity to meet those standards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the issue isn't that local authorities run elections, but whether they have the resources to do it?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: Exactly. They do a good job overall, but they need to be able to devote the people and resources the work requires.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: Clear laws can help. The rules governing the Civil Service Commission are a good example of legislation that gives us a workable role. In nearly five years in this job, I haven't felt undue pressure from politicians or civil servants.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: But organisations are weakened if vacancies aren't filled promptly or budgets aren't provided. My term ends in February and the appointment process for my successor hasn't yet set interview dates. We should avoid a gap in leadership.

chapters.title: Leaving public service and independence
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses want clearer oversight of former public officials, while recognising that independence also depends on funding and practical support.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: The Electoral Commission has said paper ballots are an important safeguard. Why not use more automatic counting?

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: Technology can make some parts of voting faster, but paper ballots are visible and can be checked by candidates, their representatives and election staff from start to finish. That helps voters and, especially, losing candidates trust that the count was fair.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: We face tens of thousands of cyberattacks on the Commission each month. That doesn't mean technology has no place: electronic check-in at polling stations is working well in many places, and automatic voter registration could help reach up to eight million eligible people who aren't registered. But those systems need strong cyber protection and clear rules.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Some senior officials can move into businesses affected by decisions they once helped make. The former advisory committee for business appointments didn't cover everyone, and its advice wasn't binding. What's changed?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: That former committee closed a year ago. The Civil Service Commission now handles decisions for civil servants and some special advisers; a separate adviser deals with politicians. Some military and intelligence-service ranks still aren't covered by our remit.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: The Cabinet Office owns the rules. We're preparing a review of how transparent and timely decisions are and how well risks are assessed. We've started making clearer to applicants who decides and how long the process should take.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Our review found that military officers and some Crown servants, including people in the intelligence agencies, also fall outside the main arrangements. We recommended better Cabinet Office oversight and updating the rules so they cover everyone consistently.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Independence is essential to our credibility. We have political members who can challenge us if they think we're too close to government, and Parliament's scrutiny matters too. But we still rely on the Cabinet Office for staff support, accommodation and funding.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Is there anything that would make your organisations more visibly independent of the government's goodwill?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: The Electoral Commission needs legal authority because it regulates elections and can impose penalties. A legal basis also means Parliament must be involved in changing its powers, but the law can be slow to adapt when circumstances change.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Whether an organisation should have legal protection depends on its job. Bodies that investigate cases or impose penalties need strong independence. I think the adviser on ministerial standards should now have a legal basis, given the investigations and advice that role is expected to provide.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: But a legal basis doesn't guarantee effective powers. The law on registering lobbying is so limited that only a small share of lobbying is currently recorded. Rules also need to be kept up to date.

chapters.title: Standards, codes and accountability
chapters.takeaway: Members questioned whether codes and existing institutions prevent serious failures; witnesses agreed that standards must shape everyday decisions, not just sit on paper.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: We've heard that the system is in a good place, but serious failures such as infected blood, Hillsborough, the Post Office and Grenfell have happened despite official codes. Are the standards working? And should government departments have a statutory monitoring officer, as local councils do?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: The Commission oversees recruitment, departures and complaints about the Civil Service Code, but it doesn't oversee every decision made inside departments. Senior officials must be held accountable when they make decisions. The Cabinet Secretary has also said civil servants should be judged on whether their work improves things.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: Some of the failures I mentioned are recent. The Cabinet Secretary's published objectives are welcome, but they don't put ethics and standards at the centre.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: The Cabinet Secretary has said she wants to review the Civil Service Code. Staff surveys show 93% of civil servants know about the code and whom to approach. That awareness matters, though leadership must make the standards real in practice.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: I'm not satisfied with the system. In many public inquiries, someone inside the organisation knew something was wrong. Defensive cultures can stop warnings being acted on, and the public's trust in institutions has been damaged.

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: Codes only help if they guide decisions every day. Our work should help public bodies review their codes, explain their values clearly and show staff how to use them. It will take sustained effort, not a quick fix.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: The proposed law would require each public body to have its own code. Is that the right approach, and will you consider a monitoring officer for central government?

turns.speaker: Doug Chalmers
turns.text: I'll take away the question about monitoring officers; we haven't gathered evidence on it. On codes, one template won't suit every organisation. A code should reflect what that organisation does and the people affected by it, so developing one requires consultation and tailoring.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: Does it help for an organisation to be established by law? And is the Civil Service's political neutrality threatened when its leaders speak about contentious issues?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: For the Electoral Commission, legal authority is necessary because we regulate and can penalise breaches. But once rules are in law, updating them can take time. The answer is to make laws carefully and keep them fit for a changing world.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: A legal safeguard prevents special advisers from taking part in civil-service appointments. On neutrality, civil servants can have personal views; impartiality means doing their professional job fairly and serving the elected government. If someone can't do that, they may need to leave the profession.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: The Civil Service must also remember what needs to continue regardless of which party is in power. In recent years I've served under five Prime Ministers and three Cabinet Secretaries. That constant change makes it important to understand the Civil Service's continuing duties.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Does serving the government of the day also mean protecting the Civil Service's ability to serve future governments? Sometimes an official's concern about a decision is made formal through a ministerial direction.

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: A request for a ministerial direction can show that a senior official believes a decision is wrong, but recognises that the elected government ultimately decides.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: Why can officials formally raise concerns about value for money, but not about standards?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: I need to think about that; it could have wider implications.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: How important is Civil Service impartiality to democracy, and is it under threat?

turns.speaker: Baroness Stuart of Edgbaston
turns.text: It's essential. Civil servants should explain what a government can do and the risks involved, including when a policy is radical. Ministers ultimately decide, but the Civil Service provides continuity and professional advice. That balance will always be debated; it depends on institutions having the resources and independence to do their jobs.

chapters.title: Election reform and who should vote
chapters.takeaway: The Electoral Commission is preparing for major reforms but wants clearer investigative powers and more evidence before advising on compulsory voting.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What work will the Electoral Commission need to do for the Representation of the People Bill, and is anything missing?

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: The bill will shape much of our work in 2027 and 2028. We expect to oversee candidates' compliance with new rules, which means building systems and helping tens of thousands of candidates understand what they need to do. We'll also support the changes on votes at 16 and voter registration.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: A lot of detailed rules will still need to be made after the bill becomes law. We would like election laws to be brought together and simplified, rather than adding more layers.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: We also need broader powers to obtain information. The bill would let us seek information from regulated participants and about party income and spending, but not enough to assess possible offences by unregulated participants or investigate some questions involving donors and newer forms of finance.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: Would compulsory voting, as used in Australia, be worth considering here?

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: We last studied it about 15 years ago. If Parliament takes the idea forward, we'd gather current evidence, including from Australia, before advising. The British context may be different.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Should the Commission be able to bring criminal cases itself, or should that remain with the police and prosecution service?

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: We don't want the power to bring private prosecutions. We support parties and candidates, and it would be difficult to combine that role with prosecuting them. We use data to spot possible breaches and pass evidence to the police or prosecutors, who have the specialist powers to investigate and bring cases.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: It may be time to look again at the Australian system, including the high level of public support there for compulsory voting.

turns.speaker: Vijay Rangarajan
turns.text: Compulsory voting is only one part of Australia's approach. They also work hard to register everyone and spend heavily to encourage people to vote. We should first improve registration here, then judge what lessons from Australia could work for us.

turns.speaker: John Pullinger
turns.text: We'd want to test the evidence for Britain, including whether compulsory voting and the cost of encouraging people to vote fit our circumstances.
